title: Book of Documents (Shujing / Shangshu)
creator: zhou-court-scribes
location: Compiled in Zhou China; earliest excavated chapters on Warring States bamboo slips (Tsinghua University)
note: The oldest Chinese 'history': speeches, oaths and proclamations attributed to the sage kings and the founders of the Xia, Shang and Zhou.
description: The Book of Documents is one of the Five Classics of Confucianism. Its chapters, arranged by dynasty, present the words of rulers and ministers at decisive moments, such as the Duke of Zhou's addresses justifying the overthrow of the Shang by the 'Mandate of Heaven'. Its textual history is unusually tangled: much was lost in the Qin burning of books, a 'New Text' version of twenty-eight or twenty-nine chapters survived through the Han scholar Fu Sheng, and an expanded 'Old Text' version appeared in the fourth century AD. The Qing scholar Yan Ruoqu demonstrated that the additional Old Text chapters were later forgeries, and the bamboo manuscripts acquired by Tsinghua University in 2008 have added previously unknown 'documents' style texts. Despite these layers, the book shaped Chinese political thought for two millennia.
image_caption: Early manuscript of the Old Text Shangshu (Tokyo National Museum)

title: Zuo Commentary (Zuozhuan)
creator: zuo-qiuming
location: Compiled in the state of Lu or its neighbours; transmitted in manuscript and later printed editions
note: The great narrative companion to the Spring and Autumn Annals, covering 722–468 BC with speeches, battles and portents.
description: The Spring and Autumn Annals record the events of the state of Lu in bare one-line entries; the Zuozhuan, traditionally attributed to Zuo Qiuming, fills them out with detailed narratives of diplomacy, war, ritual and court intrigue across all the Zhou states. Its set speeches, dramatic battle accounts such as Chengpu and Bi, and foreshadowing omens became models of Chinese prose. Unlike the Gongyang and Guliang commentaries, which explain the moral 'praise and blame' hidden in the Annals' wording, it is mainly a work of history, and modern scholars think it was compiled independently from older sources and later aligned with the Annals. It is the richest source for the Spring and Autumn period and one of the Thirteen Classics.
image_file: Li Yuanyang Zuo zhuan first page.png
image_caption: First page of a Ming-dynasty edition of the Zuozhuan

title: Discourses of the States (Guoyu)
creator: zuo-qiuming
location: Compiled in Warring States China; earliest commentary by Wei Zhao (3rd century AD)
note: Speeches and dialogues from eight states of the Spring and Autumn period, arranged state by state.
description: The Guoyu gathers the counsel of ministers and rulers of Zhou, Lu, Qi, Jin, Zheng, Chu, Wu and Yue, from the tenth to the fifth century BC, in twenty-one chapters. Where the Zuozhuan narrates events, the Guoyu centres on speeches that argue for ritual propriety and humane government. Sima Qian attributed it to a blind Zuo Qiuming, and it was long called the 'outer commentary' to the Spring and Autumn Annals, but its varied style suggests several compilers. The longest sections concern Jin and the struggle between Wu and Yue. Its speeches are an important source for early Chinese political and religious ideas.

title: Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji)
creator: sima-qian
location: Written at the Han court, Chang'an
note: China's first general history, from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu of Han, and the model for every later standard history.
description: Begun by Sima Tan and completed by his son Sima Qian, the Shiji spans some two and a half thousand years in 130 chapters divided into five sections: twelve basic annals of dynasties and rulers, ten chronological tables, eight treatises on topics such as rites, music, the calendar, waterways and economics, thirty hereditary houses of feudal lords, and seventy biographies and collective accounts. The biographies range from Confucius and Laozi to assassins, wandering knights, merchants, jesters and foreign peoples such as the Xiongnu. Sima Qian's critical use of sources, his comments signed 'the Grand Historian says', and his sympathy for the defeated give the work extraordinary moral depth. It was circulating by the first century BC, became the first of the Twenty-Four Histories, and is equally a classic of Chinese prose.
image_caption: Page of a traditional printed edition of the Shiji

title: Letter to Ren An (Bao Ren An shu)
creator: sima-qian
location: Written in Chang'an; preserved in the Book of Han and the Wenxuan anthology
note: Sima Qian's letter explaining why he endured castration rather than die before finishing his history.
description: Replying to his friend Ren An, who was awaiting execution, Sima Qian recounts the Li Ling affair, his punishment and the humiliation he has lived with since. He explains that he chose to live because his history was unfinished, and lists earlier men, Confucius, Qu Yuan, Zuo Qiuming, Sunzi and others, who wrote their great works out of adversity. He describes his aim as to examine the boundary between heaven and humanity, to understand the changes of past and present, and to make a school of his own. The letter is one of the most moving documents of Chinese literature and the key to its greatest history's purpose.

title: Strategies of the Warring States (Zhanguo ce)
creator: liu-xiang
location: Compiled by Liu Xiang in the Han imperial library, Chang'an
note: Persuasions, plots and diplomacy of the Warring States strategists, edited by Liu Xiang from palace manuscripts.
description: In the imperial library Liu Xiang found manuscripts with titles such as 'Plans of the States' and 'Long Book', containing speeches and stories of the travelling persuaders who advised the rulers of the Warring States. He arranged them by state into thirty-three chapters, from the fifth century to the Qin unification. The stories, featuring strategists such as Su Qin and Zhang Yi, celebrate cunning, eloquence and realpolitik, which made the book suspect to Confucian moralists but a favourite of writers. Sima Qian used much of the same material. A silk manuscript of related persuasions found at Mawangdui in 1973 confirmed the age of its sources.
image_caption: Page of a printed edition of the Zhanguo ce

title: Lessons for Women (Nüjie)
creator: ban-zhao
location: Written at the Eastern Han court, Luoyang
note: Ban Zhao's seven short chapters of advice to the women of her family, the founding text of Chinese women's instruction.
description: Ban Zhao wrote the Lessons for Women in old age, addressing her daughters and nieces about to marry. Its seven sections, on humility, husband and wife, respect and caution, womanly qualifications, devotion, obedience, and harmony with in-laws, teach modesty, diligence and accommodation within the household. The text joined the 'Four Books for Women' and was widely printed in China, Korea and Japan, where it was used in women's education into the twentieth century. It was criticised in the May Fourth era as a charter of female subordination; recent scholars read it in its court context and note its plea that girls, like boys, should be educated.

title: Book of Han (Hanshu)
creator: ban-gu
location: Written at the Eastern Han court, Luoyang
note: The history of the Former Han dynasty (206 BC – AD 23), the first history of a single dynasty.
description: Ban Biao began a continuation of the Shiji; his son Ban Gu reorganised it into a history of the Former Han alone, and his daughter Ban Zhao and the scholar Ma Xu completed it after Ban Gu's death in 92. It keeps Sima Qian's structure but drops the hereditary houses, with twelve annals, eight tables, ten treatises and seventy biographies. Its treatises are its glory: they cover law, food and money, geography, the five elements, rites and music, and in the 'Treatise on Literature' preserve the catalogue of the Han imperial library. The Book of Han set the template for the official dynastic history, and its sober style and orthodox Confucian tone were long preferred to the Shiji by court scholars.
image_file: 前漢書宋福唐郡庠刻宋元遞修本.jpg
image_caption: Song-dynasty printed edition of the Book of Han, with Song and Yuan repairs

title: Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi)
creator: chen-shou
location: Written in Western Jin China; commentary by Pei Songzhi, 429
note: The history of the Wei, Shu and Wu kingdoms (c. 184–280), source of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
description: Chen Shou divided his history into three books, thirty chapters on Wei, fifteen on Shu and twenty on Wu, giving imperial annals only to Wei, which the Jin regarded as the legitimate predecessor. His account of figures such as Cao Cao, Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang is spare and balanced. In 429 Pei Songzhi added a commentary that roughly doubled the text with extracts from more than two hundred other works, most now lost, so that the combined book is a treasury of third-century sources. Its section on the eastern barbarians contains the 'Account of the People of Wa', describing Queen Himiko of Yamatai, which is the starting point for early Japanese history. The fourteenth-century novel built on it made its characters household names across East Asia.
image_file: A Fragment of Biography of Bu Zhi History Books of Three Kingdoms 01 2012-12.JPG
image_caption: Early manuscript fragment of the Records of the Three Kingdoms, biography of Bu Zhi, found in Xinjiang

title: Gwanggaeto Stele
creator: jangsu
location: Ji'an, Jilin province, China, near the tomb of King Gwanggaeto
note: A 6.4-metre stone inscribed with Goguryeo's founding legend and King Gwanggaeto's conquests, the oldest major Korean historical text.
description: King Jangsu set up the stele two years after his father's death. Its roughly 1,800 Chinese characters on four faces recount the descent of the founder Jumong from the Lord of Heaven and the daughter of the river god, list the campaigns of Gwanggaeto (r. 391–412) against Baekje, the Wa (Japanese), the Khitan and others, and end with regulations for the households guarding the royal tombs. Rediscovered in the 1870s and first studied through rubbings made for the Japanese army, it became the focus of a long dispute: a passage on the Wa crossing the sea in 391 was read by prewar Japanese scholars as evidence of Japanese rule in southern Korea, while Korean and Chinese scholars have proposed other readings and questioned whether rubbings were altered. Most scholars today read the passage within Goguryeo's own propaganda against Baekje. The stele is part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Koguryo capital cities and tombs.
image_caption: The Gwanggaeto Stele at Ji'an, Jilin, in its protective pavilion

title: Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu)
creator: fan-ye
location: Written in Liu Song China, Jiankang (Nanjing)
note: The standard history of the Eastern Han dynasty (AD 25–220), admired for its style and its new collective biographies.
description: Fan Ye wrote ten annals and eighty chapters of biographies, synthesising about a dozen earlier histories of the Eastern Han. He added new categories, including the biographies of eunuchs, of the scholars persecuted in the 'partisan prohibitions', of recluses and of exemplary women, which reflected his interest in moral character. His planned treatises were never written because of his execution; in the sixth century Liu Zhao attached thirty chapters of treatises from Sima Biao's earlier history. The work contains the earliest Chinese reference to an embassy from 'Da Qin', the Roman Empire, in 166, and records a gold seal given to a king of Na in Wa in 57, a seal believed to have been found in Kyushu in 1784.
image_caption: Southern Song printed edition of the Book of the Later Han (Shaoxing era)

title: Tang Code (Tanglü shuyi)
creator: zhangsun-wuji
location: Promulgated at the Tang court, Chang'an; earliest fragments from Dunhuang and Turfan
note: The penal code of the Tang dynasty with its official commentary, the oldest complete Chinese code and the model for East Asian law.
description: The Tang Code, revised several times in the seventh century, contains 502 articles in twelve sections, from general principles and the 'ten abominations' through palace security, households and marriage, fraud, assault and theft to judicial procedure. In 653 a commission under Zhangsun Wuji added an official subcommentary that explains each article with questions and answers. The code grades punishments according to the relationships of offender and victim, building Confucian family hierarchy into law, and specifies five standard punishments from beating to death. It served as the basis of the Song, Ming and Qing codes and was adapted in Japan's Taihō and Yōrō codes, Goryeo law and the Vietnamese Lê code, making it one of the most influential legal texts in world history.

title: Taihō Code (Taihō ritsuryō)
creator: fujiwara-no-fuhito
location: Promulgated at the court of Emperor Monmu, Fujiwara-kyō; text lost, reconstructed from the Yōrō Code
note: The code that established Japan's centralised, Chinese-style ritsuryō state.
description: Compiled by a commission under Prince Osakabe and Fujiwara no Fuhito and modelled on the Tang codes, the Taihō Code consisted of penal laws (ritsu) and administrative statutes (ryō). It defined a hierarchy of ministries and ranks headed by the Council of State, divided the country into provinces and districts, and set out the allocation of rice land to households, taxes in kind and labour, conscription and the registration of the population. The original text does not survive; it is known largely through the Yōrō Code of 718, enforced in 757, and its ninth-century commentaries, the Ryō no gige and Ryō no shūge. Although many provisions decayed within two centuries, the ritsuryō framework formally lasted until the Meiji era and shaped Japanese court titles and offices for over a thousand years.

title: Generalities on History (Shitong)
creator: liu-zhiji
location: Written at the Tang History Office, Chang'an
note: The first comprehensive critique of historical writing, analysing the forms, methods and failings of earlier histories.
description: The Shitong is divided into inner chapters on the genres and components of history, such as annals, biographies, treatises, comments and prefaces, and outer chapters on the history of historical writing and on errors in specific works. Liu Zhiji argued for factual accuracy, consistency, economy of language and freedom from flattery or superstition, and he questioned the reliability of revered texts, including the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Book of Documents, which brought him criticism from orthodox Confucians. He also recommended treatises on cities, clans and local products. Little read for centuries, the Shitong was revived by Qing evidential scholars and has been compared with the historiographical theory of the European Renaissance, which it precedes by eight hundred years.

title: Chronicles of Japan (Nihon Shoki)
creator: prince-toneri
location: Presented at the court of Empress Genshō, Heijō-kyō (Nara); oldest manuscripts from the 8th–9th centuries
note: Japan's first official history, written in classical Chinese, from the age of the gods to 697.
description: The Nihon Shoki opens with two scrolls on the creation of the world and the age of the gods, often quoting alternative versions with 'one book says', and then narrates the reigns of the emperors year by year to the abdication of Empress Jitō in 697. Compared with the Kojiki of 712 it is longer, more Chinese in language and form, and more concerned with foreign relations, especially with the Korean kingdoms of Baekje, Silla and Goguryeo, drawing on lost Baekje chronicles. Its early chronology is legendary, extended to place the founding of the state in 660 BC, and its accounts of the peninsula are read critically alongside Korean and Chinese sources. From the seventh century on it becomes increasingly reliable. Lectured on at court from 721, it became the basis of Shinto and national history, and modern historians read it both as evidence and as an ideological construction of the Yamato state.
image_caption: Tanaka manuscript of the Nihon Shoki, scroll 10, 9th century (Nara National Museum)

title: Continued Chronicles of Japan (Shoku Nihongi)
creator: rikkokushi-compilers
location: Compiled at the court of Emperor Kanmu, Heian-kyō (Kyoto)
note: The second of the Six National Histories, covering the Nara period from 697 to 791.
description: Compiled in several stages and completed in 797 by Fujiwara no Tsugutada and Sugano no Mamichi, the Shoku Nihongi records the century of the Nara court: the building of Heijō-kyō, the Taihō and Yōrō codes, the casting of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji, the rise of the monk Dōkyō and the move of the capital under Emperor Kanmu. Written in classical Chinese, it preserves sixty-two imperial edicts (senmyō) in a script recording the Japanese language, invaluable for the history of the language. It is far more sober and documentary than the Nihon Shoki and is the indispensable source for eighth-century Japan.
image_file: De drie zonen van Hasetsukabe, een voorbeeld uit het Vervolg van de kronieken van Japan Hasetsukabe sanshi - Shoku Nihongi (titel op object) Vierentwintig Japanse voorbeelden van kinderlijke gehoorzaamheid voor de Honc, RP-P-1958-453.jpg
image_caption: Woodblock print illustrating a story of filial piety from the Shoku Nihongi (Rijksmuseum)

title: Historical Records of the Five Dynasties (Xin Wudai shi)
creator: ouyang-xiu
location: Written privately by Ouyang Xiu; adopted as an official history after his death
note: Ouyang Xiu's private history of the turbulent Five Dynasties (907–960), written as a moral judgement on an age of disloyalty.
description: Ouyang Xiu wrote this history on his own initiative over many years, modelling its terse judgements on the Spring and Autumn Annals. Each section begins with a lament introduced by the exclamation 'Alas!', and he grouped officials into categories such as those who died for their dynasty and those who served several houses, condemning the latter, notably the statesman Feng Dao who served ten rulers. After his death the court ordered it printed in 1077, and it was later ranked among the official standard histories alongside the older Five Dynasties history of Xue Juzheng. Its moral approach influenced Song and later ideas of loyalty, and it is admired as prose.

title: New Book of Tang (Xin Tangshu)
creator: ouyang-xiu
location: Compiled at the Song court, Kaifeng
note: The Song re-writing of the history of the Tang dynasty, by Ouyang Xiu and Song Qi.
description: Dissatisfied with the Old Book of Tang compiled in 945, the Song court commissioned a new history in 1044. Song Qi wrote most of the biographies and Ouyang Xiu the annals, treatises and tables; it was presented in 1060. The authors added treatises on the military, examinations and official selection, and expanded the tables of chancellors and genealogies, but compressed many documents and speeches into the terse 'ancient-style' prose they championed. Critics have long noted that the Old and New histories complement each other, the older one preserving more original documents and the newer offering more systematic treatises and fuller coverage of the late Tang. Both are counted among the Twenty-Four Histories.
image_file: 宋刻本《石壁精舍音注唐书详节》卷一及卷二百.jpg
image_caption: Song-dynasty printed abridgement of the Tang histories with phonetic notes

title: Comprehensive Mirror to Aid in Government (Zizhi tongjian)
creator: sima-guang
location: Compiled in Luoyang and presented at the Song court, Kaifeng
note: A year-by-year history of China from 403 BC to AD 959, the most celebrated chronological history in Chinese.
description: Sima Guang conceived the work as a single, readable narrative of statecraft to replace the sprawl of the dynastic histories. Emperor Yingzong authorised the project in 1066 and Emperor Shenzong gave it its title, 'mirror for aiding government'. Working with Liu Shu, Liu Ban and Fan Zuyu, Sima Guang first assembled a 'long draft' of all sources arranged by date, then cut it down, writing a thirty-chapter Examination of Discrepancies to explain his choices among conflicting sources. The finished work covers the sixteen dynasties from the Warring States to the end of the Five Dynasties, with Sima Guang's comments on the lessons of each episode. It was the favourite history of emperors and officials in China, Korea and Japan, inspired abridgements and continuations, and Mao Zedong is said to have read it many times.
image_caption: Page from an edition of the Zizhi tongjian

title: The Great Mirror (Ōkagami)
creator: heian-anonymous-authors
location: Written in Heian-kyō (Kyoto); author unknown
note: A vernacular history of the Fujiwara regents from 850 to 1025, told by two very old men in conversation.
description: The Ōkagami is framed as a dialogue overheard at a Buddhist service at the Urin'in temple in Kyoto, where two men said to be about 190 and 180 years old reminisce about the reigns and the great ministers they have seen, while a young samurai questions them. Organised like a Chinese composite history, with sections on emperors, ministers and anecdotes, it centres on Fujiwara no Michinaga, whose power and splendour it celebrates while also recording rivals, scandals and ironies. The dialogue form lets it present differing views, and its lively anecdotes about figures such as Sugawara no Michizane became famous. It was the first of the 'four mirrors' (shikyō), followed by the Imakagami, Mizukagami and Masukagami, and a model for vernacular Japanese history.

title: History of the Three Kingdoms (Samguk sagi)
creator: kim-busik
location: Compiled at the Goryeo court, Gaegyeong (Kaesong); earliest complete printing 1512, Gyeongju
note: Korea's oldest surviving history, covering Silla, Goguryeo and Baekje.
description: Commissioned by King Injong and compiled by Kim Busik with ten assistants, the Samguk sagi follows the Chinese composite form: twenty-eight gwon of basic annals for the three kingdoms, three of chronological tables, nine of treatises on rites, music, costume, carriages, households, geography and offices, and ten of biographies of generals, scholars, loyal subjects and rebels, including Kim Yu-sin and Eulji Mundeok. Kim drew on lost Korean records as well as Chinese histories, and added his own Confucian commentary. Nationalist historians later accused him of treating Silla as the centre and of deferring to China; other scholars stress that he wanted Koreans to know their own history as well as China's. It remains the foundation of Korean ancient history.
image_caption: Printed edition of the Samguk sagi

title: Outline and Details of the Comprehensive Mirror (Tongjian gangmu)
creator: zhu-xi
location: Planned by Zhu Xi and completed by his disciples, notably Zhao Shiyuan
note: Zhu Xi's restructuring of the Comprehensive Mirror into moral 'outlines' and narrative 'details', the standard popular history of late imperial East Asia.
description: Zhu Xi admired Sima Guang's history but disagreed with some of its judgements, notably its treatment of Cao Cao's Wei rather than Liu Bei's Shu Han as the legitimate dynasty of the Three Kingdoms. He designed a work in which brief headings in large characters, framed in the 'praise and blame' language of the Spring and Autumn Annals, state the moral meaning of each event, followed by details in smaller characters. His students completed the 59 chapters, and it was printed in 1219. Under the Ming and Qing it was enlarged, issued in imperial editions and widely taught; in Korea and Japan it shaped the writing of national histories such as An Jeong-bok's Dongsa gangmok and the Honchō tsugan. Modern historians value it less as a source than as evidence of how Neo-Confucians read the past.

title: Jottings of a Fool (Gukanshō)
creator: jien
location: Written in Kyoto or on Mount Hiei on the eve of the Jōkyū War
note: Jien's interpretation of Japanese history through changing 'principles' (dōri), the first Japanese philosophy of history.
description: The Gukanshō opens with a chronological table of Chinese and Japanese rulers, then narrates Japanese history from the first emperor, Jinmu, to Jien's own day, with growing detail on the twelfth-century wars between the Taira and Minamoto. Jien explains the past as the working out of principles that change with each age, within the Buddhist scheme of decline, and argues that in his own time the court, the Fujiwara regents and the warriors of Kamakura must cooperate. Written in Japanese with katakana rather than classical Chinese, so that it would be understood, it is also an implicit warning against the plans of the retired emperor Go-Toba, whose rising against Kamakura in 1221 failed. It is valued as an insider's view of court politics and as a pioneering work of historical reflection.

title: Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms (Samguk yusa)
creator: iryeon
type: Collection of history and legend (5 gwon)
location: Compiled at Ingaksa, Gunwi; earliest surviving printings from the early Joseon period
note: Iryeon's collection of foundation myths, Buddhist legends, songs and local traditions of ancient Korea.
description: Where the Samguk sagi is a Confucian official history, the Samguk yusa gathers what it left out. It opens with a chronological table and a section on 'wonders' beginning with the earliest account of Dangun, said to have founded Gojoseon after the union of a son of the heavenly lord with a bear-woman, and continues with stories of the kings of the three kingdoms and Gaya, the introduction and spread of Buddhism, eminent monks, miracles, pagodas and images, and acts of filial piety. It preserves fourteen hyangga, the oldest Korean vernacular poems, written in Chinese characters used for their sounds. Compiled in the aftermath of the Mongol invasions, it is often seen as an affirmation of Korean identity. It is the essential source for Korean mythology and early Buddhism.
image_file: Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms in museum.jpg
image_caption: Early printed edition of the Samguk yusa in a museum display

title: Mirror of the East (Azuma Kagami)
creator: kamakura-shogunate-compilers
location: Compiled in Kamakura; main manuscript lineages include the Hōjō and Kikkawa copies
note: The official chronicle of the Kamakura shogunate from 1180 to 1266, in diary form.
description: The Azuma Kagami records the history of the warrior government in Kamakura day by day, from Minamoto no Yoritomo's rising in 1180 to the return of the sixth shogun, Prince Munetaka, to Kyoto in 1266. Written in a Japanese style of classical Chinese, it draws on shogunal documents, court diaries and the records of vassal families, and includes the text of many orders and petitions. It presents the Hōjō regents favourably and is silent on some awkward events, and some years are missing. Despite this it is the basic source for the early warrior age, and later regimes, including the Tokugawa, consulted it as a manual of warrior government.
image_caption: Page from a manuscript of the Azuma Kagami

title: Comprehensive Examination of Literature (Wenxian tongkao)
creator: ma-duanlin
location: Compiled in Leping, Jiangxi; printed under the Yuan
note: An encyclopaedic history of Chinese institutions from antiquity to the Song, under twenty-four headings.
description: Ma Duanlin built on Du You's Tongdian of 801 and Zheng Qiao's Tongzhi of the twelfth century, the other two of the 'Three Comprehensives' (santong). His categories run from land tax, currency, population, labour service, markets and tribute through schools, examinations, offices, rites, music, military affairs and punishments to bibliography, imperial genealogy, geography and foreign peoples. Under each he arranged the documentary record (wen) and the discussions of officials and scholars (xian), then gave his own analysis. His preface argues that while political events are unique, institutions develop continuously and must be studied over the long term. The work was continued under the Ming and Qing and remains a standard reference for Chinese economic and administrative history.

title: Chronicle of the Direct Descent of Gods and Sovereigns (Jinnō shōtōki)
creator: kitabatake-chikafusa
location: Written at Oda castle, Hitachi province, for the young Emperor Go-Murakami
note: Kitabatake Chikafusa's defence of the Southern Court through a history of the imperial succession from the gods.
description: Composed during the civil war between the Southern Court of Go-Daigo's line and the Northern Court backed by the Ashikaga, the Jinnō shōtōki opens with the declaration that great Japan is the land of the gods, and then reviews each reign. Chikafusa argues that Japan alone has preserved an unbroken divine succession, but that true legitimacy lies in the 'direct line' marked by virtue and possession of the three sacred regalia, which for him meant the Southern Court. He also judges rulers and ministers by Confucian standards of virtue. Widely copied in the Edo period, the work influenced the Mito school and Meiji nationalism, and its ideas were used in prewar ideology; modern scholars read it as a political text of its civil-war moment.

title: History of Yuan (Yuanshi)
creator: song-lian
location: Compiled at the Ming court, Nanjing
note: The official Ming history of the Mongol Yuan dynasty, compiled in under a year.
description: The Hongwu Emperor ordered the history of the Yuan in 1369 to proclaim that its mandate had ended. Song Lian and Wang Wei led a team that worked from the Yuan veritable records and the administrative compendium Jingshi dadian, producing the first draft in 188 days and completing it in 1370 after a second session to cover the last reign. Its haste caused duplications and inconsistent renderings of Mongol and Central Asian names, but it preserves many Yuan documents verbatim, including much on the empire's institutions, Tibetan Buddhism and the Grand Canal. Modern scholarship combines it with Persian sources such as Rashid al-Din and with the Secret History of the Mongols.
image_file: 元史二百卷目录二卷 国子监.jpg
image_caption: Imperial Academy (Guozijian) printed edition of the History of Yuan

title: Annals of the Joseon Dynasty (Joseon wangjo sillok)
creator: joseon-historiographers
location: Compiled in Hanseong (Seoul); copies kept in mountain archives (Jeongjoksan, Taebaeksan, Odaesan, Jeoksangsan); now in Seoul National University and other repositories
note: The day-by-day official record of twenty-five Joseon reigns, from 1392 to 1863, one of the most detailed dynastic records in the world.
description: After each king's death a compilation office gathered the draft records of the court historians, the Royal Secretariat diaries and government documents and produced the annals of the reign, which were printed in a few copies and sealed in archives; the drafts were then washed out so that the paper could be reused and the historians protected. The annals cover politics, diplomacy, economy, natural phenomena, rituals and the arts in great detail, from King Taejo to King Cheoljong. Only one set survived the Japanese invasions of 1592, and copies were remade and dispersed to remote mountain archives; one set taken to Tokyo in the colonial period was largely destroyed in the 1923 earthquake, and surviving volumes were returned to Korea in 2006. The records of the last two reigns, compiled under Japanese rule, are not usually counted. The annals were registered in UNESCO's Memory of the World in 1997.
image_file: Joseon Wangjo Sillok and its case in museum.jpg
image_caption: Volumes of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty with their storage case

title: Songs of the Dragons Flying to Heaven (Yongbi eocheonga)
creator: jeong-in-ji
location: Compiled at the Joseon court, Hanseong (Seoul)
note: The first work written in Hangul, celebrating the ancestors of the Joseon royal house and the dynasty's founding.
description: Commissioned by King Sejong and composed by Jeong In-ji, Gwon Je and An Ji, the cycle of 125 cantos praises six generations of the founding family, from Yi Seong-gye's ancestors to Taejo and Taejong, pairing their deeds with those of Chinese founders to show that Joseon held the Mandate of Heaven. Each canto is given in Korean, in the new alphabet, followed by a Chinese version and extensive historical annotations. Written before the alphabet's public promulgation, it served as a trial of the script and as dynastic legitimation, and its notes are a valuable source for the history of the Joseon founding and the Korean language.

title: Hunminjeongeum Haerye (Explanations and Examples of the Correct Sounds)
creator: sejong
location: Issued at the Joseon court, Hanseong (Seoul); the only known original copy is in the Gansong Art Museum, Seoul
note: The document announcing and explaining Hangul, the Korean alphabet created by King Sejong.
description: King Sejong announced his new script in the last month of 1443, and in 1446 it was promulgated with this explanatory edition. It opens with Sejong's own preface, explaining that the people cannot write their language in Chinese characters and that he has made twenty-eight letters that are easy to learn and use daily, followed by short descriptions of the letters. The explanations by scholars of the Hall of Worthies set out how consonant shapes imitate the organs of speech and how vowels are built from symbols of heaven, earth and humanity, with examples, and Jeong In-ji's postface describes the purpose of the work. The book was lost for centuries until a copy was found in Andong in 1940 and acquired by the collector Jeon Hyeong-pil, who protected it through the colonial period and the Korean War. It is a Korean National Treasure and on UNESCO's Memory of the World register, and its date is celebrated as Hangul Day.
image_caption: Pages of the Hunminjeongeum Haerye, 1446 (Gansong Art Museum)

title: History of Goryeo (Goryeosa)
creator: jeong-in-ji
location: Compiled at the Joseon court, Hanseong (Seoul)
note: The official Joseon history of the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392).
description: The new Joseon dynasty began writing Goryeo's history soon after its founding in 1392, but successive drafts were rejected over questions of how to present the fall of Goryeo and the founding of Joseon and whether to keep Goryeo's imperial-style terminology. The final version, presented by Jeong In-ji and others in 1451, uses the Chinese composite form with forty-six gwon of 'hereditary houses' for the kings, reflecting the status of a tributary kingdom rather than imperial annals, together with treatises, tables and biographies, including chapters on 'rebels' that present the last Goryeo kings unfavourably. A companion chronological history, the Goryeosa jeolyo, followed in 1452. Despite its Joseon viewpoint it is the essential source for Goryeo history, especially its treatises on land, military and government.
image_caption: Printed volumes of the Goryeosa (National Museum of Korea)

title: Record of the Countries across the Eastern Sea (Haedong jegukgi)
creator: sin-suk-ju
location: Compiled at the Joseon court, Hanseong (Seoul)
note: A Joseon description of Japan and the Ryukyu kingdom, with maps and diplomatic regulations.
description: Ordered by King Seongjong, the Haedong jegukgi drew on Sin Suk-ju's own journey to Japan in 1443 and on Joseon diplomatic records. It describes the geography and provinces of Japan, the succession of its emperors and shoguns, the major lords and island rulers who sent missions to Korea, customs and languages, and the Ryukyu kingdom, and lays down the rules for receiving Japanese envoys and traders in the three ports open to them. Its maps are among the earliest surviving printed maps of Japan and Ryukyu. Sin's closing advice to maintain peaceful relations with Japan was recalled with regret after the invasions of the 1590s.

title: War Diary (Nanjung ilgi)
creator: yi-sun-sin
location: Kept aboard ship and in camp; autograph manuscripts at Hyeonchungsa shrine, Asan
note: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's diary of the Imjin War, recording battles, strategy and private grief.
description: Yi Sun-sin kept the diary from the start of the Japanese invasion in 1592 until shortly before his death at Noryang in November 1598. The surviving autograph volumes record naval preparations, the battles of Okpo, Hansan, Myeongnyang and others, weather and sea conditions, discipline, supplies, relations with Ming allies and quarrels with rival commanders and the court. They also record his worry for his mother, his grief at her death and at the killing of his son Yi Myeon, and his illness and sleeplessness. The title, meaning 'diary in the midst of war', was given when it was edited in 1795. It is a Korean National Treasure and was inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World in 2013.
image_caption: Autograph volumes of the Nanjung ilgi with Yi Sun-sin's letters and reports (Hyeonchungsa)

title: Book of Corrections (Jingbirok)
creator: ryu-seong-ryong
type: Memoir and history of the Imjin War
location: Written at Hahoe, Andong; autograph manuscript preserved by the Ryu family; printed 1633 and 1647; Kyoto edition 1695
note: Ryu Seong-ryong's account of the Japanese invasions of 1592–98, written so that Korea would learn from its mistakes.
description: The title takes a line from the Book of Songs about being chastened by past errors in order to guard against future trouble. Ryu begins with the diplomatic exchanges with Toyotomi Hideyoshi before the war, including the divided reports of the envoys sent to Japan in 1590, then narrates the fall of Busan and Seoul, the king's flight to the north, the arrival of the Ming armies, Yi Sun-sin's naval victories and the long negotiations and second invasion. He frankly describes the failures of the government, including his own, and the suffering of the people. The autograph manuscript is a Korean National Treasure, and the work was printed in Japan in 1695, where it was read as a source on Hideyoshi's wars.
image_caption: Manuscript of the Jingbirok

title: Diaries of the Royal Secretariat (Seungjeongwon ilgi)
creator: seungjeongwon-secretaries
location: Kept in the palace, Hanseong (Seoul); now in the Kyujanggak Institute, Seoul National University
note: The daily record of the Joseon king's office, surviving for nearly three centuries and far larger than the Annals.
description: The Royal Secretariat recorded the king's daily activities, audiences, memorials received, orders issued and even weather each day, and each month's record was bound as a volume. Records before 1623 were destroyed in the Japanese invasions and in later palace fires, but 3,243 volumes from the reign of King Injo to the end of the Korean Empire survive, containing an estimated 240 million characters. Because they were not edited like the Annals, they preserve the language of court exchanges and much detail omitted elsewhere, including meteorological data used by modern climate scientists. The diaries were inscribed in UNESCO's Memory of the World in 2001, and a modern translation project has been under way for decades.
image_caption: Volumes of the Seungjeongwon ilgi (National Treasure No. 303)

title: Strengths and Weaknesses of the Provinces of the Realm (Tianxia junguo libing shu)
creator: gu-yanwu
location: Compiled by Gu Yanwu; circulated in manuscript and printed in the 19th century
note: Gu Yanwu's vast compilation on the geography, defence, water control, taxation and economy of each region of Ming China.
description: Gu Yanwu began this work as a young man in the last years of the Ming, reading through gazetteers, histories and official documents to extract information on the practical condition of every province. After the Manchu conquest he continued it during his travels in the north. Arranged by region, it gathers material on fortifications, garrisons, rivers and canals, land registration, salt, coastal defence and trade, with Gu's comments on the causes of strength and weakness. It is a monument of the turn from philosophy to practical, evidence-based learning that marked the early Qing and an essential source for late Ming social and economic history.

title: Comprehensive Mirror of Our Realm (Honchō tsugan)
creator: hayashi-razan
location: Compiled at the Hayashi school, Edo, for the Tokugawa shogunate
note: The shogunate's chronological history of Japan to 1611, modelled on Sima Guang's Comprehensive Mirror.
description: Ordered by the shogunate in 1644, the history was begun by Hayashi Razan as the Honchō hennenroku and, after a fire and Razan's death in 1657, completed by his son Hayashi Gahō with a large staff in 1670. Written in classical Chinese, it covers Japanese history from the age of the gods to the accession of Emperor Go-Mizunoo, treating the early myths with Confucian rationalism. One passage, which recorded the theory that the imperial line descended from the Chinese Wu Taibo, is said to have angered Tokugawa Mitsukuni and spurred his rival Dai Nihonshi. The Honchō tsugan established Japanese history as a field of Confucian scholarship under the Tokugawa.

title: Reading History and Its Lessons (Tokushi yoron)
creator: arai-hakuseki
location: Based on lectures given to the shogun Tokugawa Ienobu in Edo
note: Arai Hakuseki's rational account of how power passed from the imperial court to the warrior houses.
description: Hakuseki explains Japanese history from the ninth century to the founding of the Tokugawa shogunate as a series of 'nine changes' in the government of the realm by the court and 'five changes' in rule by warriors, culminating in the Tokugawa peace. He looks for causes in the actions and abilities of rulers and ministers rather than in fate or the gods, and judges the decline of the court as a consequence of its own failings. The work served to justify Tokugawa rule historically, and is admired as one of the most analytical pre-modern Japanese histories.

title: Great History of Japan (Dai Nihonshi)
creator: tokugawa-mitsukuni
location: Compiled at the Shōkōkan, Mito domain (Edo and Mito)
note: The Mito domain's vast history of Japan from Emperor Jinmu to 1392, a source of imperial loyalism.
description: Begun by Tokugawa Mitsukuni in 1657 and continued by the Mito domain and later the Tokugawa family for two and a half centuries, the Dai Nihonshi follows the composite form of the Chinese standard histories: annals of emperors, biographies, treatises and tables. Its annals and biographies were largely finished by 1715; the treatises and tables were completed only in 1906. It is known for three judgements: listing Empress Jingū among consorts rather than sovereigns, recognising Prince Ōtomo as Emperor Kōbun, and treating the Southern Court as legitimate. Its research into documents set high standards, and the 'Mito learning' it fostered, emphasising loyalty to the emperor, fed the late Edo movement that overthrew the shogunate.
image_caption: Printed volumes of the Dai Nihonshi

title: Tidings of the West (Seiyō kibun)
creator: arai-hakuseki
location: Written in Edo; circulated privately in manuscript
note: Hakuseki's record of his interrogation of the Italian missionary Sidotti, a pioneering Japanese study of Europe.
description: In 1708 the Sicilian priest Giovanni Battista Sidotti landed secretly on Yakushima, disguised as a samurai, hoping to revive Christianity in Japan. Brought to Edo, he was questioned by Arai Hakuseki in 1709. Hakuseki recorded his answers on European geography, politics and customs and on Christian doctrine. He admired Sidotti's learning and recommended that he be sent home rather than executed; Sidotti was instead confined and died in 1714. The book, kept within official circles, combined respect for Western knowledge with rejection of Christianity, and became a foundation of Edo Western learning.

title: Told Round a Brushwood Fire (Oritaku shiba no ki)
creator: arai-hakuseki
location: Written in Edo after Hakuseki's retirement
note: Arai Hakuseki's memoir of his family and his years in government, a landmark of Japanese autobiography.
description: Written after the death of the shogun Ietsugu and Hakuseki's loss of office, the memoir begins with portraits of his stern samurai father and his childhood studies, then gives a detailed, self-justifying account of the policies he pursued for Ienobu and Ietsugu: currency reform, judicial cases, the regulation of the Nagasaki trade and his reforms of protocol for the Korean embassy. Intended for his descendants, it is an insider's view of shogunal government and a portrait of a Confucian statesman's mind, and it is often regarded as the first great Japanese autobiography.

title: History of Ming (Mingshi)
creator: zhang-tingyu
location: Compiled at the Qing court, Beijing
note: The official Qing history of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), the last of the Twenty-Four Histories.
description: The Qing opened a History Office for the Ming in 1645 and relaunched it in 1679 with scholars recruited through a special examination, many of them sons of Ming loyalists. The private scholar Wan Sitong, who refused office, shaped the draft for two decades, and Wang Hongxu's version became the basis of the final text presented by Zhang Tingyu in 1739. It is praised for its organisation and its treatises, and includes chapters on eunuchs, corrupt officials and 'roving bandits'. Its treatment of the Manchu rise and of southern Ming resistance was constrained by Qing sensitivities, and contemporary literary inquisitions punished unauthorised Ming histories. With it the canon of the Twenty-Four Histories was declared complete in the Qianlong reign.

title: Annotated Account of Korean History (Dongsa gangmok)
creator: an-jeong-bok
location: Written in Gwangju, Gyeonggi province
note: An Jeong-bok's critical history of Korea from Gija Joseon to the end of Goryeo, the summit of Silhak historiography.
description: An Jeong-bok adopted the outline-and-details form of Zhu Xi's Gangmu to write a moralised but carefully researched chronological history of Korea. He set out a scheme of legitimate succession running from Dangun and Gija through Mahan and Unified Silla to Goryeo, examined conflicting sources and recorded his doubts, and appended studies of historical geography and questions of dating. Encouraged by his teacher Yi Ik, he aimed to free Korean history from reliance on Chinese accounts. The work circulated in manuscript and was printed only in the early twentieth century; it is regarded as the most rigorous Korean history before modern scholarship.

title: Complete Library of the Four Treasuries (Siku quanshu)
creator: ji-yun
location: Compiled at the Qing court, Beijing; seven manuscript sets, of which the Wenyuan Pavilion copy is now in the National Palace Museum, Taipei
note: The Qianlong Emperor's manuscript collection of some 3,460 works in about 36,000 volumes, with an annotated catalogue of over ten thousand titles.
description: In 1773 the Qianlong Emperor ordered a search for books across the empire and the copying of the most important into a single library, arranged in the four traditional divisions of classics, histories, philosophers and belles-lettres. Hundreds of scholars under Ji Yun and Lu Xixiong collated texts, including several hundred works recovered from the Ming Yongle Encyclopedia, and thousands of copyists produced seven sets housed in purpose-built pavilions. The annotated catalogue, the Siku quanshu zongmu tiyao, reviews each work. The project also served the court's political aims: works judged hostile to the Manchus or to imperial authority were altered, excluded or destroyed, and historians debate how to weigh its preservation of learning against this censorship. Several sets were lost in the Taiping and other wars; four survive.
image_file: The Complete Library in Four Sections (Siku Quanshu) WDL3020.jpg
image_caption: Manuscript volume of the Siku quanshu (World Digital Library)

title: General Principles of Literature and History (Wenshi tongyi)
creator: zhang-xuecheng
location: Written in various posts in China; first printed by Zhang's son in 1832
note: Zhang Xuecheng's essays arguing that the classics are history and that historical writing needs insight, not just learning.
description: Zhang Xuecheng wrote these essays over three decades, against the dominant evidential scholarship of the Qianlong era. He argued that the Six Classics were the records and institutions of the ancient kings, so that the Way could be found only in historical change; that great history required 'historical virtue' and a grasp of meaning beyond accumulation of detail; and that local gazetteers should be designed as serious histories of their regions. He distinguished records kept for reference from interpretive histories written to convey understanding. Neglected until the late Qing, the essays were championed in the twentieth century and are now read alongside Vico and Herder as a major philosophy of history.
image_file: 上海会文堂版文史通义，章学诚故居陈列.jpg
image_caption: Shanghai Huiwentang edition of the Wenshi tongyi, displayed in Zhang Xuecheng's former residence

title: Unofficial History of Japan (Nihon gaishi)
creator: rai-sanyo
location: Written in Kyoto; first printed in Osaka and Kyoto
note: Rai San'yō's dramatic history of the warrior houses, the best-selling history of late Edo Japan.
description: Organised around the great families, from the Taira and Minamoto through the Hōjō, Kusunoki, Ashikaga, Oda and Toyotomi to the Tokugawa, the Nihon gaishi is written in vigorous classical Chinese with frequent comments by the author. It praises warriors who served the emperor faithfully, such as Kusunoki Masashige, and quietly frames the shogunate as delegated imperial authority. Circulated in manuscript and then printed, it became essential reading for the young samurai of the loyalist movement of the 1850s and 1860s and a school text in the Meiji era. Modern historians regard it as literature rather than critical history.
image_file: Титульный лист Нихон гайси 1874 года издания.jpg
image_caption: Title page of an 1874 edition of the Nihon gaishi

title: Letter to Queen Victoria
creator: lin-zexu
location: Written at Canton (Guangzhou); English translations printed in the Chinese Repository and the London press
note: Lin Zexu's open letter asking the British queen to stop her subjects' opium trade with China.
description: In 1839 Lin Zexu, as imperial commissioner at Canton, wrote to Queen Victoria arguing that the opium trade was poisoning China while Britain itself banned the drug, and asking her to forbid its cultivation and export. The letter appeals to a shared moral order and warns that foreign merchants caught with opium would be punished under new Qing laws. Translated into English, it was published in Canton and London, though there is no evidence the queen ever received it. Its mixture of moral argument and the Qing tributary framework, which treated Britain as a distant vassal, has made it a classic document for teaching the clash between Chinese and Western ideas of international order on the eve of the Opium War.

title: Gazetteer of the Four Continents (Sizhou zhi)
creator: lin-zexu
location: Compiled at Canton (Guangzhou) from translated Western sources
note: Lin Zexu's compilation of translated information on the countries of the world, basis of Wei Yuan's Haiguo tuzhi.
description: During his time at Canton Lin Zexu employed translators, among them Liang Jinde, to render Western newspapers, legal texts and books into Chinese, so that he could understand his opponents. The core of the Sizhou zhi is a translation of parts of Hugh Murray's Encyclopaedia of Geography, describing the geography, governments and customs of the countries of Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas. Lin passed the manuscript to Wei Yuan when he went into exile, and it became the core of the Haiguo tuzhi. It marks the first serious Qing effort to gather systematic knowledge of the West.

title: Treaty of Nanking
creator: nanking-treaty-negotiators
location: Signed aboard HMS Cornwallis at Nanjing, 29 August 1842
note: The treaty ending the First Opium War, which opened five ports to British trade and ceded Hong Kong Island.
description: The Treaty of Nanking's thirteen articles required the Qing to pay twenty-one million silver dollars, open Canton, Amoy (Xiamen), Fuzhou, Ningbo and Shanghai to British residence and trade with consuls, cede Hong Kong Island in perpetuity, abolish the Cohong merchant monopoly and conduct official correspondence on equal terms. The supplementary Treaty of the Bogue (1843) added extraterritoriality and most-favoured-nation treatment, and similar treaties with the United States and France followed in 1844. In Chinese historiography it marks the beginning of the 'century of humiliation' and of the unequal treaties; in Britain it was long seen as opening China to free trade. Hong Kong was returned to China in 1997.
image_file: The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking.jpg
image_caption: John Platt, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846

title: Record of the Sacred Wars (Shengwu ji)
creator: wei-yuan
location: Written in Yangzhou; first printed 1842
note: Wei Yuan's history of the military campaigns of the Qing dynasty, written in the shadow of the Opium War.
description: Completed in the year the Treaty of Nanking was signed, the Shengwu ji narrates the Qing conquest and campaigns from the dynasty's founding to the early nineteenth century, including wars against the Zunghars, in Tibet, Burma and Vietnam, and against rebellions such as the White Lotus. Wei Yuan drew on archives he had access to in Beijing and on official compilations, and added essays on military finance, organisation and coastal defence. By recalling the dynasty's past strength and analysing its decline, he argued for reform of the military and administration. It was widely read and reprinted, including in Japan.

title: Illustrated Treatise on the Maritime Kingdoms (Haiguo tuzhi)
creator: wei-yuan
type: Geography and history of the world
location: Compiled at Yangzhou; first edition in 50 chapters, final edition in 100
note: The first great Chinese survey of the Western world, urging China to learn Western technology to defend itself.
description: Wei Yuan expanded Lin Zexu's translated Gazetteer of the Four Continents with Chinese and Western sources into a geography and history of the world, arranged by ocean and continent, with maps, descriptions of governments and religions, and essays on maritime defence and the manufacture of ships and guns. His famous strategy was to learn the superior techniques of the foreigners in order to control them. The book went through three editions, reaching 100 chapters in 1852. It reached Japan in the 1850s, where it was reprinted many times and read by reformers in the years of Perry's arrival, while in China it influenced the Self-Strengthening officials of the 1860s.
image_caption: Page from the Haiguo tuzhi

title: Conditions in the West (Seiyō jijō)
creator: fukuzawa-yukichi
location: Published in Edo/Tokyo
note: Fukuzawa Yukichi's clear account of Western governments, economies and social institutions, a bestseller of the Meiji Restoration.
description: Drawing on his travels and on English and American books, including a Chambers's educational text on political economy, Fukuzawa described in plain Japanese how Western countries were governed and how their schools, hospitals, newspapers, banks, steam engines and postal systems worked, with sketches of the history of the United States, Britain, the Netherlands and other countries. The first volume included a translation of the American Declaration of Independence. Said to have sold some quarter of a million copies including pirated editions, it informed both the new government and ordinary readers and shaped the vocabulary of Meiji reform.
image_caption: Title page of Seiyō jijō, 1866

title: Charter Oath (Gokajō no goseimon)
creator: yuri-kimimasa
location: Proclaimed by Emperor Meiji at the Shishinden, Kyoto Imperial Palace, 6 April 1868
note: The five-article oath announcing the programme of the new Meiji government.
description: In the early months of the Boshin War the new government sought to win the support of the domains and to signal a break with the shogunal past. Yuri Kimimasa's draft, revised by Fukuoka Takachika and Kido Takayoshi, was sworn by the fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji before the gods in the presence of the court and daimyo. Its five articles promised that deliberative assemblies would be established and affairs decided by public discussion, that all classes would unite, that common people would be allowed to pursue their callings, that 'evil customs of the past' would be abandoned, and that knowledge would be sought throughout the world. Its wording was vague enough to be cited both by the government and by the movement for popular rights, and in 1946 Emperor Shōwa quoted it in his New Year rescript.
image_caption: The Charter Oath in the official manuscript

title: True Account of the Ambassadors' Tour of America and Europe (Bei-Ō kairan jikki)
creator: kume-kunitake
location: Published by the Daijōkan, Tokyo
note: Kume Kunitake's record of the Iwakura Mission of 1871–73, a detailed Japanese survey of Western civilisation.
description: The Iwakura Mission, led by Iwakura Tomomi with Kido Takayoshi, Ōkubo Toshimichi and Itō Hirobumi, travelled for nearly two years through the United States and Europe to study institutions and seek revision of the unequal treaties. Kume, its official chronicler, wrote a five-part account describing factories, parliaments, schools, prisons, cities and landscapes, illustrated with copperplate engravings, and reflecting on what Japan should adopt. He noted that Europe's lead was recent, a matter of decades rather than centuries, an observation that encouraged Meiji modernisers. It is a key source for how the Meiji leadership saw the West.

title: Constitution of the Empire of Japan (Meiji Constitution)
creator: ito-hirobumi
location: Promulgated in Tokyo, 11 February 1889; in force 29 November 1890; original in the National Archives of Japan
note: Asia's first modern written constitution, establishing a constitutional monarchy with an elected Diet.
description: Drafted in secret by Itō Hirobumi with Inoue Kowashi, Itō Miyoji and Kaneko Kentarō, with advice from the German jurists Hermann Roesler and Albert Mosse, the constitution was presented as a gift from the emperor to his subjects. Its seventy-six articles declared the emperor sacred and inviolable and the source of sovereignty, with supreme command of the army and navy, while creating a bicameral Imperial Diet with an elected lower house, a cabinet and courts, and guaranteeing rights 'within the limits of law'. It allowed both the party governments of the 1920s and the military dominance of the 1930s. It remained in force until replaced in 1947 by the Constitution of Japan, which was adopted formally as its amendment.
image_caption: Opening of the Constitution of the Empire of Japan with the imperial seal (National Archives of Japan)

title: Commentaries on the Constitution of the Empire of Japan (Kenpō gige)
creator: ito-hirobumi
location: Published in Tokyo under Itō Hirobumi's name; English translation by Itō Miyoji, 1889
note: The authoritative official commentary on the Meiji Constitution, article by article.
description: Prepared largely by Inoue Kowashi and issued under Itō's name, the Kenpō gige explains each article of the Meiji Constitution, presenting the emperor's sovereignty as rooted in Japan's unbroken imperial line while describing the Diet, cabinet and courts as instruments of constitutional government. An English translation by Itō Miyoji appeared the same year to present Japan's new order to Western powers. It was the starting point for later debates between scholars such as Hozumi Yatsuka, who emphasised imperial sovereignty, and Minobe Tatsukichi, whose theory of the emperor as an organ of the state dominated in the 1920s before being banned in 1935.

title: Treaty of Shimonoseki
creator: ito-hirobumi
location: Signed at the Shunpanrō inn, Shimonoseki, 17 April 1895
note: The treaty ending the First Sino-Japanese War, by which China recognised Korean independence and ceded Taiwan to Japan.
description: Negotiated by Itō Hirobumi and Mutsu Munemitsu for Japan and Li Hongzhang for the Qing, after Li had been wounded by a Japanese assailant during the talks, the treaty required China to recognise the full independence of Korea, ending the tributary relationship; to cede Taiwan, the Penghu Islands and the Liaodong peninsula; to pay an indemnity of 200 million taels; and to open further ports to Japanese trade. Within days Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to return Liaodong in exchange for a larger indemnity, the Triple Intervention. The treaty marked Japan's emergence as an imperial power, began fifty years of Japanese rule in Taiwan and stimulated reform movements in China. It is remembered very differently in Japan, China, Taiwan and Korea.
image_caption: The Treaty of Shimonoseki, 17 April 1895, with the signatures and seals of the plenipotentiaries

title: New Historiography (Xin shixue)
creator: liang-qichao
location: Serialised in Xinmin congbao (New Citizen Journal), Yokohama
note: Liang Qichao's manifesto calling for a history of the Chinese nation and its people in place of dynastic histories.
description: Written in exile in Japan, New Historiography argued that traditional histories recorded courts rather than nations, individuals rather than groups, past facts rather than present relevance, and events rather than ideas. Liang proposed that history should trace the evolution of the national group and discover the principles of its progress, drawing on Social Darwinism and Japanese and European historiography. The essay also coined or popularised concepts such as the 'Chinese nation' and a periodisation into ancient, medieval and modern. It launched the movement for a 'new history' in China and influenced both Nationalist and Marxist historians.

title: A New Reading of History (Doksa sillon)
creator: sin-chae-ho
location: Serialised in Daehan maeil sinbo, Seoul
note: Sin Chae-ho's call for a national history of Korea centred on the Korean people rather than on dynasties or China.
description: Written as Korea fell under Japanese protectorate rule, A New Reading of History argued that a nation's history is the story of its people's rise and fall, and that Korean history should centre on the descendants of Dangun through Buyeo and Goguryeo rather than on Silla and Chinese-derived figures such as Gija. Sin criticised Kim Busik and the Confucian historiographers for subordinating Korea to China, and Japanese historians for distorting the Korean past. Unfinished in its serial form, it was nevertheless the manifesto of nationalist historiography. His later Early History of Korea (Joseon sanggosa), serialised in 1931, developed its ideas with the theory of history as struggle between self and non-self.

title: Imperial Edict of the Abdication of the Qing Emperor
creator: empress-dowager-longyu
location: Issued in Beijing, 12 February 1912
note: The edict ending more than two thousand years of imperial rule in China and transferring authority to a republic.
description: After the Wuchang uprising of October 1911 most provinces declared independence, and a provisional republican government under Sun Yat-sen was formed in Nanjing. Negotiations led by Yuan Shikai produced terms under which the Qing court would abdicate in return for favourable treatment of the imperial family, the Manchus, Mongols, Muslims and Tibetans. The edict, issued by the Empress Dowager Longyu on behalf of the six-year-old Puyi, declares that the will of the people has turned to a republic and charges Yuan Shikai with organising a provisional government; drafting is traditionally credited to the reformer Zhang Jian with revisions by Yuan's circle. Historians discuss the edict as a constitutional document that linked the Qing territories to the new republic.
image_caption: The abdication edict of 1912

title: Korean Declaration of Independence (Gimi dongnip seoneonseo)
creator: march-first-signatories
location: Read at Taehwagwan and Tapgol Park, Seoul, 1 March 1919; printed at the Bosŏngsa press
note: The declaration of the March First Movement proclaiming Korea's independence from Japanese rule.
description: Inspired in part by the principle of national self-determination proclaimed at the end of the First World War and by the death of the former emperor Gojong in January 1919, religious leaders secretly prepared a declaration drafted by Choe Nam-seon and printed in some twenty thousand copies. It proclaims Korea an independent state and Koreans a free people, appeals to justice and humanity rather than hatred, argues that independence would serve the peace of East Asia, including Japan's true interest, and closes with three pledges to act in an orderly, peaceful way. Its reading on 1 March set off demonstrations involving hundreds of thousands across Korea and among Koreans abroad, which were suppressed with many deaths and arrests. The movement led to the founding of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in Shanghai in April 1919, and 1 March is a national holiday in South Korea.

title: Methods for the Study of Chinese History (Zhongguo lishi yanjiufa)
creator: liang-qichao
location: Lectures at Nankai University, Tianjin, published in Shanghai
note: Liang Qichao's systematic guide to modern historical research, a founding text of the Chinese discipline.
description: Based on lectures of 1921, the book defines history as the record of human activity in society, surveys the Chinese historiographical tradition from the Shiji to Zhang Xuecheng, and sets out how historians should collect, criticise and interpret sources, including archaeology, inscriptions and non-Chinese records. It combines Western methods, drawn in part from the French manual of Langlois and Seignobos, with Qing evidential scholarship. A supplementary volume followed in 1926. It was widely used as a textbook and shaped the training of Chinese historians in the Republican period.

title: Three Principles of the People (Sanmin zhuyi)
creator: sun-yat-sen
location: Delivered as lectures in Guangzhou, January–August 1924
note: Sun Yat-sen's programme of nationalism, democracy and the people's livelihood, the ideology of the Republic of China.
description: Sun had outlined the three principles since 1905; in 1924, with his manuscripts lost in an earlier rebellion, he gave sixteen lectures setting them out in full, leaving the last principle incomplete at his death. Nationalism called for unity of the Chinese and an end to foreign domination; democracy combined popular rights with a government of five branches, adding examination and control to the executive, legislative and judicial; livelihood proposed equalisation of land rights and regulation of capital. The principles are cited in the constitution of the Republic of China, open its national anthem, and were also accepted, with different emphasis, by the Chinese Communist Party during the alliances of the 1920s and 1930s.

title: Debates on Ancient History (Gushi bian)
creator: gu-jiegang
location: Published in Beijing and Shanghai
note: The collected essays and controversies of the Doubting Antiquity school, which challenged the traditional history of ancient China.
description: The first volume, edited by Gu Jiegang in 1926, opens with a long autobiographical preface explaining how his study of folk songs and drama led him to see ancient history as legend accumulated in layers. Later volumes, edited with Luo Genze, Lü Simian and others, gathered essays by dozens of scholars debating the dates and authenticity of the classics, the historicity of Yu the Great, and the origins of the Five Emperors. The collection made source criticism central to Chinese ancient history, though later archaeology and excavated manuscripts led some scholars to call for 'walking out of the age of doubt'. As a twentieth-century work it remains in copyright.

title: Early History of Korea (Joseon sanggosa)
creator: sin-chae-ho
location: Serialised in the Chosun Ilbo, Seoul; first book edition 1948
note: Sin Chae-ho's history of ancient Korea, opening with his definition of history as the struggle between self and non-self.
description: Written in exile and serialised while Sin was in prison, the Joseon sanggosa covers Korean history from Dangun to the fall of Baekje and Goguryeo. Its introduction defines history as the record of the struggle between the self (a) and the non-self (bi-a), and argues that a people must know its own past to survive. Sin stressed the extent of ancient Korean states in Manchuria, criticised Confucian historians for subordinating Korea to China and challenged colonial Japanese scholarship. Later scholars have questioned some of his geographical claims while acknowledging his role in founding modern Korean historiography. It is studied in both North and South Korea.

title: Constitution of Japan (Nihonkoku kenpō)
creator: constitution-of-japan-drafters
location: Promulgated in Tokyo, 3 November 1946; in force 3 May 1947; original in the National Archives of Japan
note: Japan's postwar constitution, establishing popular sovereignty, fundamental rights and the renunciation of war.
description: Adopted as a formal amendment to the Meiji Constitution, the Constitution of Japan makes the emperor a symbol of the state and of the unity of the people, deriving his position from the will of the people, with whom sovereignty resides. It guarantees civil liberties, equality of the sexes, academic freedom and social rights, establishes parliamentary cabinet government and an independent judiciary, and in Article 9 renounces war as a sovereign right and the maintenance of armed forces for that purpose. The interpretation of Article 9, under which Japan has maintained Self-Defence Forces since 1954, has been debated ever since, as has whether the constitution should be revised. It has never been amended, making it one of the oldest unamended constitutions in the world.
